meta.title: Nine Charts About Wealth Inequality in America
meta.description: Explore how wealth inequality has varied across race, age, and time in the US over the past 60 years, what’s driving inequities, and how policymakers can close these gaps and help all Americans build wealth.

intro.value: Behind the current affordability crisis is another economic reality: wealth inequality is higher in the United States than in almost any other developed country and is not improving. In this context, it’s understandable why many Americans feel our economic system is rigged against them.
It’s more important than ever that all Americans have opportunities to build wealth and improve their lives. But for generations, those opportunities haven’t been equally shared.

That doesn’t have to be the case going forward. In the nine charts below, we lay out the current and historical data and bold solutions needed to ensure all Americans can reach long-term economic prosperity.

The first three charts show how the opportunities wealth brings have differed over time and by race and age since 1963. The remaining charts show how gaps in earnings, homeownership rates, retirement savings, emergency savings, benefits from tax subsidies, and intergenerational wealth transfers contribute to differences in opportunity. We also identify evidence-based solutions that federal, state, and local policymakers can implement to rebuild paths to true economic mobility in the US.

sections.subhead: Wealth is increasing but so is inequality.

content.value: In the past 60 years, the distribution of wealth has largely shifted from the middle class to the wealthiest families, increasing wealth inequality. In 1963, the wealthiest families had $1.9 million more in wealth than families in the middle of the wealth distribution, but by 2025, they had $16.1 million more.
Between 1963 and 2025,

• families near the bottom of the wealth distribution (at the 10th percentile) went from having $25 in debt to $210 in wealth,
  • those in the middle (at the 50th percentile) nearly quadrupled their wealth (from $55,373 to $216,100),
  • those near the top (at the 90th percentile) saw their wealth increase more than sevenfold (from $322,374 to $2.5 million), and
  • the wealthiest families—those wealthier than 99 percent of all families—saw their wealth increase more than eightfold (from $2.0 million to $16.3 million).

sections.chart_source: Urban Institute calculations from the Survey of Financial Characteristics of Consumers 1962, the Survey of Changes in Family Finances 1963, and the Survey of Consumer Finances 1983–2025.
sections.chart_notes: 2025 dollars. We used inflation adjustment factors from Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025: Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances (PDF). No comparable data are available between 1963 and 1983.

sections.subhead: Wealth gaps by race and ethnicity are large.

content.value: In general, average wealth for US families has grown steadily since 1963, aside from drops in 2010 and 2013 associated with the Great Recession. But the differences in wealth held by white, Black, and Hispanic families have also generally grown in recent decades.

In 1983, the average white family had about $350,000 more in wealth than the average Black and Hispanic families. By 2025, white families had over $1.3 million more in wealth ($1.7 million) than Black families ($242,500) and Hispanic families ($334,800). Put another way, white families had seven times the average wealth of Black families and five times the average wealth of Hispanic families.

Looking at the most recent years of data, we see that Black families are the only group whose median net worth fell from 2022 to 2025 (from $48,300 to $36,400). But their average net worth increased over the same period. These data suggest inequality is growing both within this group and between racial and ethnic groups.

In 2022, the Survey of Consumer Finances disaggregated data for Asian families for the first time. Their average wealth was $2.0 million and $2.2 million in 2022 and 2025, respectively, which is 1.3 times the average wealth of white families in those years. However, more-disaggregated analyses by country of origin and ethnic group point to large differences in wealth among Asian Americans.

The differences in wealth discussed here are the result of exclusionary policies, programs, and institutional practices that facilitate opportunities for white families to build wealth while creating barriers to wealth for families of color. Below we focus on solutions that ensure all families, especially those who have faced challenges, can access and build wealth.

sections.subhead: The wealth gap between Black and white families widens with age.

content.value: Families of all races and ethnicities accumulate wealth over their lives. But on average, white families build more wealth than Black or Hispanic families in the same age group, widening the wealth gap at older ages.

Consider those born between 1943 and 1951. When they were roughly in their thirties in 1983, white families had, on average, $198,900 more in wealth—equal to three times more wealth—than Black families. By 2025, when they were in their midseventies and early eighties, that gap had surpassed $1.7 million, and the average white family had more than four times the wealth of the average Black family.

sections.chart_source: Urban Institute calculations from the Survey of Consumer Finances 1983–2025.

In 2025, these people were ages 74 to 82, and in 1983, they were ages 32 to 40. We used inflation adjustment factors from Changes in U.S. Family Finances from 2022 to 2025: Evidence from the Survey of Consumer Finances (PDF).

sections.subhead: Differences in lifetime earnings lead to differences in wealth.

content.value: Money saved from earnings helps many workers build wealth, but earnings differ by race and gender. In 2025, the average white man age 61 to 65 had earned $3.4 million over his career, while the average Black or Hispanic man had earned $2.1 million. Women earn less overall, but gaps remain: the average white woman had earned $2.0 million, the average Black woman $1.5 million, and the average Hispanic woman $985,500.

Having high income and going to college are not enough to overcome these differences. Even at higher income levels, racial wealth gaps remain. People of color often have more family financial responsibilities and receive fewer inheritances, so having a higher income may not be enough to accumulate wealth at a similar rate as white families. And among people who have a bachelor’s degree, all women of color earn less on average than white women, and all men of color earn less on average than white men.

One factor that contributes to these differences is employment discrimination. It results in occupational crowding, where women and people of color with similar education levels are crowded into lower-quality, lower-paying jobs and crowded out of higher-quality jobs. Uneven pay for identical roles and caregiving responsibilities (PDF) also create earnings disparities.
POLICY SOLUTIONS

To close earnings gaps, policymakers could focus on improving access to high-quality, well-paying jobs at every age; enhancing educational and training opportunities; and combating wage discrimination.
Federal

• Standardize data collection on pay and conduct proactive audits to detect and combat payment discrimination.
  • Raise the federal minimum wage. Had the minimum wage been $15 an hour in 2022, affected families would have seen average earnings increase by $5,600 a year, and 7.6 million people would have exited poverty.
  • Expand unemployment insurance and reemployment assistance.
State and Local

• Consider labor regulations that support job quality, such as paid sick time, paid family and medical leave, and fair scheduling protections.
  • Leverage workforce investments to offer sector-based skills training for in-demand jobs and improve access to higher-paying jobs.
  • Raise wage and labor standards for government contractors.

sections.subhead: Policies have not made progress on homeownership gaps, a key source of wealth inequality.

content.value: Historically, homeownership has been the main way people have built wealth in the United States. Yet the homeownership rate has stagnated at 65 percent in recent years as housing has become increasingly unaffordable.

Estimates from 2024 suggest homeownership rates among Black families are increasing, but Black Americans remain the only racial group with a homeownership rate below 50 percent. And the homeownership gaps between white and Black families and white and Hispanic families are worse today than they were in 1960.

Differences in homeownership by race persist today partly in response to the stubborn legacy of exclusionary housing policies, such as redlining and racial covenants. In addition, racial differences in the three Cs that determine mortgage access—credit, collateral, and capacity—add to the unfair differences that discrimination created, even though they don’t explicitly include race. Moreover, real estate agent steering, industrial zoning, and appraisal partiality leave the property values and wealth-building potential of Black-owned homes lagging those of white-owned homes.
POLICY SOLUTIONS

Homeownership can provide financial stability and wealth-building opportunities. But to increase homeownership and ensure families can benefit from it, policymakers should provide supports across the entire homeownership journey that harmonize access to housing and maintenance and preservation of one’s home. Policies that could achieve better outcomes include expanding mortgage credit access, increasing the supply of affordable homes, strengthening loss mitigation efforts, providing capital for renovations, and ensuring homeowners have a suitable will or trust so their home can be passed on if they so choose.
Federal

• Implement the pilot to increase access to small-dollar mortgages under the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, with necessary capacity supports.
  • Increase lender participation in HUD’s 203(k) programs, which many lenders do not offer despite recent improvements.
  • Promote workforce development and apprenticeship programs as part of the path to unlocking new and affordable residential construction.
State and Local

• Reform local land-use and zoning policies to expand the supply of available and affordable housing.
  • Lower the cost and increase the availability of development capital.
  • Regulate rising property insurance costs.
  • Incentivize developers through the allocation of federal funds.
  • Expand down-payment assistance, particularly for first-generation homebuyers.

sections.subhead: Retirement savings have grown substantially in recent decades, but racial gaps have widened sharply.

content.value: Retirement savings provide stability and security for families as workers age out of the workforce. But racial differences in retirement savings have increased sevenfold over the past three and a half decades.

In 1989, white families had about $54,000 more in average retirement savings than Black families and about $39,000 more than Hispanic families. But by 2025, they had about $400,000 more in average retirement savings than both Black and Hispanic families. From 2022 to 2025, Asian families went from having about $20,000 less in average retirement savings than white families to having $100,000 more.

Several factors are driving differences in earnings and retirement savings. First, occupational crowding means that many women and people of color have limited access to higher-quality jobs that offer access to higher earnings and retirement plans. Second, even among families with access to retirement plans, those with lower incomes contribute smaller portions of their incomes and are more likely to withdraw money early to cover financial emergencies.
Without meaningful retirement savings, families are more likely to experience poverty and to depend on Social Security or safety net programs as their sole source of retirement income.
POLICY SOLUTIONS

To help people prepare for retirement and maintain security and stability during retirement, policymakers need holistic solutions that address wealth accumulation, housing affordability, and health costs for older adults.
Federal

• Increase access to workplace retirement savings plans through the federal Trump IRA marketplace. These plans could incorporate lessons from state automatic IRA programs to maximize their effectiveness.
  • Strengthen Social Security and expand access to private annuities to make retirement more affordable. The Social Security trust fund will be depleted by 2032 without congressional action, and annuities remain underused despite offering guaranteed lifetime income.
  • Protect older adults’ retirement savings from market volatility. Market volatility hits some retirees harder than others, particularly those with less time to recover losses.
  • Strengthen Medicare and Medicaid to reduce medical debt. About 10 percent of adults over age 50 have been found to have medical debt in collections.
State and Local

• Make it more accessible for older adults to remain in their homes. Expanding affordable housing options, improving coordination between housing and health services, and supporting home modifications that enable aging in place could help more older adults stay in their homes.
  • Increase access to retirement savings. This can be achieved by establishing government-backed universal retirement accounts, expanding access to workplace retirement savings programs, improving job quality, and encouraging employers to offer retirement plans with features that boost participation, such as automatic enrollment. State and city automatic IRAs, including OregonSaves and PhillySaves, are promising examples that serve workers without 401(k) plans.

sections.subhead: Federal and state policies discourage families with low incomes from building emergency savings.

content.value: How much savings is adequate to withstand economic shocks depends on many factors. But one month of income can be sufficient for most families enduring an unemployment spell or unexpected expense—and can even prevent financial hardship in the long term.

Yet in 2025, less than half of families (47 percent) had this amount of liquid savings, including more than half of white and Asian families (55 and 58 percent, respectively) and roughly a third of Black families and Hispanic families (29 and 35 percent, respectively). These findings suggest the vast majority of Black and Hispanic families could face hardship because of common financial emergencies. Families with unpaid credit card debt may be especially vulnerable, given that credit card debt constrains household budgets, even for those with higher incomes.

These unfair differences are the result of exclusionary policies. For example, redlining denied access to credit in majority-Black neighborhoods, even when people were personally qualified. Means testing in public benefits programs also discourages saving and participation in mainstream financial markets.
POLICY SOLUTIONS

Emergency savings are a direct way to prevent people from experiencing financial insecurity and falling into poverty. To improve access to savings products, policymakers can automate savings programs, incentivize savings, and change asset limits so they don’t prevent families with low incomes from building wealth.
Federal

• Set a universal asset limit floor for public assistance programs, and exclude 530A account assets from calculations for all benefits programs.
  • Automate enrollment in emergency savings accounts, which recent federal legislation permits. This nearly doubles the likelihood that people will save.
  • Enhance the country’s automatic stabilizers. Expanded refundable tax credits and enhanced unemployment benefits could better protect families during economic downturns.
State and Local

• Raise or eliminate asset limits in public benefits programs, as California recently initiated with its Medi-Cal program.
  • Implement matched savings programs, where a nonprofit entity, the government, or an employer rewards initial and regular deposits of liquid savings. Programs like these have been shown to increase savings and reduce hardship.
  • Implement guaranteed income programs, which can provide predictable funds to help families meet basic needs and weather unexpected events without depleting their savings or going into debt.

In addition, employers can incorporate emergency savings in employee benefits by embedding them in retirement accounts (e.g., Pension-Linked Emergency Savings Accounts) or offering stand-alone rainy-day funds—which could also improve employee well-being and retention. These are two workplace-based policies that can help employees build short-term financial safety nets.

sections.chart_title: Share of Families with Emergency Savings Equal to at Least One Month’s Income, by Race and Ethnicity, 1989–2025
sections.chart_source: Urban Institute calculations from the Survey of Consumer Finances 1989–2025.
sections.chart_notes: Emergency savings are liquid assets including money market accounts, checking accounts, savings accounts, call accounts, and prepaid cards. Income includes wage income, Supplemental Security Income, disability payments, alimony, insurance reimbursements, tax refunds, disbursements from scholarships and loans, government payments, settlements of legal claims, real estate, and lottery winnings. We follow the literature in using one month of income as the threshold (see CFPB 2022, Farrell et al. 2019, and Sabat and Gallagher 2020).

sections.subhead: Federal tax policies fail to help families with low incomes build wealth.

content.value: The federal government spends more than $360 billion on housing and retirement tax subsidies to support wealth building each year, but families don’t benefit from them equally.

More than 80 percent of these subsidies go to taxpayers in the top 40 percent of the income distribution, while taxpayers in the bottom 20 percent receive less than 0.3 percent of subsidies. Because Black and Hispanic families have lower average incomes, they receive much less of these subsidies than white families.

Many of the safety net programs that families with low incomes participate in, such as food and cash assistance, focus on income and keeping families afloat. And while many families would benefit from complementary wealth-building programs, some programs discourage saving. For instance, many families won’t qualify for Supplemental Security Income, the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or Temporary Assistance for Needy Families benefits if they have $3,000 in assets.
POLICY SOLUTIONS

To help families with low incomes build wealth, federal policymakers could make current tax subsidies more progressive. Two assets dominate the portfolios of most households with any significant savings: home equity and retirement accounts.
Federal

• Limit the mortgage interest tax deduction and redirect the revenue to provide a credit for first-time homebuyers, who today receive only a small share of mortgage borrowing.
  • Strengthen tax incentives for lower-income workers to start retirement accounts. This could be paid for by reducing the maximum contribution levels offered to higher-income workers.
  • Penalties for saving in various income- and asset-tested programs could be reduced or eliminated. Consider policies that permit and incentivize families to save while they benefit from income-based safety net programs, as the bipartisan SSI Savings Penalty Elimination Act would allow.
  • Provide families with no inherited wealth with more tax deferrals or limit their tax liability to protect their savings for the future.
State and local governments could also build on each of these efforts, just as many have done with work subsidies in the Earned Income Tax Credit.

sections.chart_source: Tax Policy Center (TPC) tables T26-0116, T26-0151, and T26-0153.
sections.chart_notes: 2026 dollars. M = million. B = billion. “Income” refers to TPC’s “expanded cash income” measure, which is described in Rosenberg (2013). The tax expenditure for retirement saving incentives is calculated using a present value approach.

sections.subhead: Wealth inequality is passed from generation to generation.

content.value: The nation is undergoing an unprecedented wealth transfer, with wealth shifting significantly from baby boomers to their heirs. In 2025, white families were three times more likely to receive an inheritance than Black families, four times more likely than Asian families, and about four times more likely than Hispanic families. Though these differences have fluctuated in size somewhat, they’ve largely persisted since 1989. Researchers estimate that intergenerational transfers explain 12 to 16 percent of the racial wealth gap.

Intergenerational wealth transfers differ by race because of unfair differences in wealth and earnings. One study showed that the shares of Black and white families who intend to leave a sizeable estate are similar, but Black families are less likely to be homeowners or to have the necessary large amounts of wealth and income to do so.

Heirs’ properties also contribute to differences in who receives an inheritance. Lacking a clear will or trust can result in heirs’ property, or a “tangled title,” where multiple descendants own undivided interests in a property. Owners of these properties can’t access equity—a challenge amplified by the concentration of homes in poor condition among inherited properties—and could lose these properties. Though heirs’ properties are a pervasive challenge, they disproportionately affect families of color.
POLICY SOLUTIONS
Policymakers can help narrow wealth disparities by facilitating intergenerational transfers, including through wills and legal property transfers.
Federal

• Incentivize states to adopt the Uniform Partition of Heirs’ Property Act to help reduce the possibility of a family experiencing property loss.
  • Authorize state funding for counseling and pro bono legal assistance.
  • Establish clear standards for serving homeowners with heirs’ property in federally funded home repair programs.
  • Provide dedicated federal funding for title-clearing legal services and estate planning.
State and Local

• Offer estate-planning assistance, particularly geared toward low-income communities, with the support of nonprofits and philanthropies.
  • Help residents navigate the legal process to resolve land-ownership disputes through legal education and heirs’ property resolution services. In the South and central Appalachia, Black families often hand land down to younger generations without legal documentation proving ownership. Families with these properties may not be able to secure a mortgage or home improvement loan but are responsible for taxes and other liabilities and can have their property taken away through court-ordered sales.
  • Expand the legal system’s capacity to address heirs’ property cases while increasing awareness among judicial system stakeholders about the Uniform Partition of Heirs’ Property Act and when to apply it.

Nonprofits can also play a role by providing estate-planning support through wills clinics and other support services, financial planners, and funds for investment and immediate debt mitigation. The private sector could also offer opportunities for will or trust creation alongside wealth-building programs.

outro.value: Promising federal policies to narrow wealth gaps

Wealth inequality in the United States is a complex and persistent challenge that requires bold policy solutions. The inequality is vast because of policy choices, and it can be reduced through policy choices, too.

The solutions above show that policymakers at all levels have a role to play in eliminating unfair racial and other wealth differences. The following federal policies could have the greatest impact, however, particularly if implemented together:

• Make 530A deposits progressive. To better position new universal early-life wealth-building accounts to reduce wealth inequality, the federal government (and philanthropies) could make deposits into the 530A accounts of children in families with low and moderate incomes that are larger than the total contributions to higher-income children's accounts.
  • Set a universal asset limit floor for public assistance programs, and exclude 530A account assets from calculations for all benefits programs.
  • Develop universal portable retirement savings accounts and ensure sufficient retirement income through Social Security.
  • Limit the mortgage interest tax deduction, and use the revenues to provide a credit for first-time homebuyers.
  • Institute national reparations policies to compensate for the legacy of slavery, the exclusion of Black-dominated occupations from Social Security, and the historical exclusion of Black people from labor, housing, and capital markets.

It will also be important for the federal government to strengthen capital income taxation and capture AI gains. To limit the potential for the rapid growth and outsized market valuations of generative AI companies to increase wealth concentration, the following strategies could expand who owns the gains from this technology, which stems and benefits from public contribution and knowledge:

• Implementing broad-based ownership structures. This would enable the public to own shares of the technology and the companies that are expanding uses of AI and its infrastructure. With this structure, any valuation accrues to a wide group of people, raising the economic floor.
  • Offering a public ownership share or equity through a tax payment.
  • Taxing the stocks of large generative AI companies and depositing the proceeds into a sovereign wealth fund that pays an annual dividend to the public. This is similar to how mining, gas, and other extractive industries pay a dividend to the communities resources are extracted from.
By addressing what’s driving economic inequality, these strategies could ensure all people have a fair shot at building wealth.

text.value: In this feature, wealth (also referred to as net worth) is total assets minus total liabilities. Assets are the sum of financial assets (such as bank accounts, stocks, bonds, and 401(k)s or IRAs) and nonfinancial assets (such as homes and real estate, businesses, and vehicles). Liabilities include both unsecured debt (such as credit card balances) and secured debt (such as mortgages and vehicle loans). Wealth includes only private command over resources: we do not include Social Security wealth or try to quantify future streams of Medicare, for example.

The majority of the data for this feature come from the Survey of Consumer Finances (SCF), which is sponsored by the Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System. The SCF is often considered the gold standard for studying wealth in the United States. It comprehensively measures many assets and debts, including less-captured items such as the value of certain kinds of pensions and life insurance on the asset side, and loans secured against retirement accounts and life insurance policies on the liabilities side.

The SCF asks respondents to self-identify their race and ethnicity. Families are classified into one of four groups based on the respondent’s selections (non-Hispanic white, non-Hispanic Black or African American, Hispanic or Latino, and other). For consistency with the survey, we refer to non-Hispanic white and Black families as “white” and “Black,” respectively, and Hispanic or Latino families as “Hispanic.” As of 2022, the SCF also separates Asian people from the “other” group. They make up about 30 percent of that group. The remaining families in the group identify as American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, Pacific Islander, another race, and more than one race, with the last subgroup making up the largest share of the remaining families. The SCF cannot disaggregate the “other” group further because of small sample sizes.
Chart 4 uses the terms men and women to describe gender, though the majority of the source data for DYNASIM were collected using male/female labeling.

The data underlying this feature have some limitations, namely our incomplete understanding of Asian families’, Native families’, and rural families’ experiences building wealth. In addition, we did not assess some wealth-building activities, including small-business ownership and stock market participation, because of the relatively small shares of Black and Hispanic wealth they represent.
